title: Breaking and Entering: Acopia on Friendship, Transience, and the Things Left Unsaid
transcript:
Avatar. And just then we heard a great remix from Daniel Avery, who was a recent guest on Breaking and Entering. The UK producer was in town for Rising Festival of Acopia's track, Be Enough. And I'm joined in the RRR studios at the moment by a couple of members of the local trio Acopia. I've got Kate Durman and Morgan Wright with me in the studio. Thanks for joining me, guys. Thanks for having us. It's a pleasure to be here. Thanks for having us. We should mention

the other member of your trio, Lachlan, unfortunately unwell and unable to join us today. But thanks very much for dropping by Breaking and Entering. I know your show has sold out at the Night Cat. So yeah, you're not here with anything to promote, just having a chat. And of course, you've been up to quite a bit recently. Some big tours with Acopia, sort of making really great waves overseas now as well. But yeah, you got back from a couple of months away on a North American tour

of UK and Europe as well. Is it nice to be sort of back in your hometown for a bit now? It is. I personally really miss the food a lot. Most of all. Oh, most of all my friends, probably. But the produce and food was a close second. But the produce and food, not to be ungrateful. It was an amazing tour and it was, yeah, a really positive experience. Yeah, so grateful to have gone there. Do you sort of have first places that you go to when you tour overseas to sort of orient

yourself in a new city? I know lots of people sort of like to start at record stores or something like that. Probably just like a good pub meal or something. Or Pret. Or Pret. Yeah, in Europe or the UK. So good. Yeah, we should do that though. That's actually wise. That sounds way smarter. Do stuff like that. How do the members of Acopia go touring together? Is it all pretty smooth sailing? It's pretty good. Now we've done a few international tours and have

spent a lot of time around each other in each other's pockets. And I would say by now we can read each other very well. For instance, you know, just noticing when we need to give each other a bit of space. Yeah, yeah, definitely. We all need quite a bit of space. So we have a lot of, we get to have a lot of like downtime and do our own thing. But yeah, always like going and eating dinners and stuff together, which is really nice. Excellent. You've described,

I guess, working with Acopia as like a surreal experience writing music with your best friends. What is it about the experience of writing together that feels, you know, so surreal or unique? I'll let you answer that, Morgan. That's for you. Thank you, Kate. I think primarily the fact that it's like really fun and actually enjoyable. I think sometimes like collaborating can be a bit of a slog. But I think what makes it really like easy for the

project is that the fact that all of us, you know, can play instruments and produce. So if we want to communicate an idea, like we can do words, but then you can also just show each other the idea. And that's like a really, I think like... Saves a lot of time and talking, I guess.

[Unclear audio at 00:03:29–00:03:31]

I guess looking back sort of over three albums that you've done together now, does your personal history and friendship sort of shape the sound of Acopia in a way that maybe you might not have anticipated? Well, I guess just like through, like I was saying, we spend a lot of time in a positive way, by the way. We spend a lot of time together and our friendship with each other is all very strong because of that and might not have been as strong if we weren't doing this project together.

[Unclear audio at 00:04:02–00:04:04]

In terms of like the sound, though.

[Unclear audio at 00:04:06–00:04:09]

I think, yeah, definitely like I feel like whenever we make music, we always spend probably a quarter of the time like debriefing emotionally about like stuff that's stressing us out. But also like talking about like just everything happening in the world. So I think like as we're like going to be affected by everything around us as humans and that's going to like impact our craft. I think like as the albums have gone along, you kind of like can communicate that maybe a bit clearer or we're all like

maybe better at like channeling like say a certain emotion or trying to elicit like a certain emotion in the listener through the songwriting or through the production. I feel like we're much better at that now. Yeah. I guess all three members are really like accomplished electronic producers in your own right too. You've had individual projects that are going on outside of Acopia. Kate with Purient, who we heard from a bit earlier in the show today. Lachlan, who isn't here, but one half of Tambo’s House with River Yarra.

And Morgan, you're, yeah, releasing music under your own name as well. And you've said that Acopia was born from a shared curiosity in the genre, sort of softer ethereal corners outside of the club space. Can you talk about, I guess, what drew you to that side of the music and yeah, how that shared interest evolved into the creative vision behind the band? Yeah, I think initially we were, we all just really wanted to make like collaborate together.

And because of like our own projects being in like the dance music world, we were kind of set on or like fixated even on having like slower songs, like 80, 90, 100 BPM. And I think like that naturally had us gravitating to like the more like potentially, especially for the first record, like having elements of like trip hop more so and like slow down breakbeats. Because we'd all been producing like faster music with breakbeats. And then we all have like a, like a strong affection for like some of the same bands, like in particular, like Radio Dept..

So I think like through, like as the records are being written and evolved, we're like starting to learn more about like one another's music tastes in the like softer side of music rather than just sharing like club tracks or, or whatever. And then COVID kind of happened maybe a year after the band had started. And I think that as well changed like the, the, the songs that we wrote and yeah, leaning into that, like more home listening, chilled out sound.

You're talking about sort of before just about, yeah, emotions. Are there specific, I guess, emotions or environments you're trying to evoke through Acopia when you're stepping away from that traditional sort of late night energy?

[Unclear audio at 00:07:21–00:07:23]

I guess it's just going inwards a bit more just in, as a whole, as a concept even. Um, and like you were saying, Morgan, about like how we kind of like debrief a lot of the time before we go into writing something. I think it's helped us become more open people. And so maybe, yeah, maybe that. Did that make sense?

[Unclear audio at 00:07:46–00:07:48]

I hope so. I've forgotten the question now. What was the question? Me too. No, you answered it very well. I guess, yeah, some people have identified your, your music as sort of having this really dreamlike quality to it as well. And you mentioned going inward, are dreams like an important source of information or inspiration for Acopia at all? I feel like maybe the, um, uh, yeah, maybe thematically sometimes, um, fragmented bits of dreams or ideas or feelings.

Um, but I mean, there's been a couple of times where I or one of us is like had a dream about a song or an idea. And, and we've worked on it, can't say it has been good, but we've done, we've done it before. Yeah. I think my dreams relating to Acopia are all just like airport related stress dreams, like forgetting my passport or something like that.

[Unclear audio at 00:08:48–00:08:51]

Your, um, album title, Blush Response, which, yeah, it was an album of the week last year, I guess references the phrase from Blade Runner. It's used in this test to distinguish, um, humans from replicants and sort of measuring their emotional reactions. What drew you, yeah, specifically to that, that concept and how does the title connect to maybe themes or emotions you're exploring on this record? I'll let you handle that one, Kate. Yeah. You came up with the idea.

Um, I was re-watching like the original Blade Runner and it's one of the phrases that they use quite early on. Um, and I just thought it was a cool concept cause it's like, yeah, trying to work out if something is like, um, what was the word? Not robot, like a replicant, um, whatever that means. Um, I, I just thought about it as like an emotional thing, like maybe some people that have, uh, difficulty with connecting to certain emotions and needing to kind of like sit with it for a bit to work out what they're really feeling or experiencing.

Um, and it's something that I've experienced before. I just thought it kind of sounded, uh, like what the album sounds like in a way. Yeah. You've also mentioned that, um, the idea of like blushing itself sort of being a really raw and involuntary thing and a true reminder that you're alive. That's yeah, I guess a really interesting idea of that blushing being that exact moment that there's an internal feeling becomes this sort of external reaction. Um, yeah, what was it about that idea that resonated so strongly and it's just really cute.

Like blushing is really cute and having a crush on someone's really cute and it makes you feel alive. And, um, a lot of our songs are like love songs or like kind of about breakup or like, um, learning who you are and what you're about. So I think it's just that really. The track we're about to hear in a minute talk about it, um, you've said explores fears of emotional intimacy and sort of the piling weight of all things left unspoken.

Can you maybe share a bit more about, about that track and why was that something you felt drawn to exploring? I think at the time I, oh, wait, maybe it was lucky at the time that I hope you won't mind me saying this. He, he, we like were in the room starting to write this idea and he was in a bit of a funk and we're like, what's going on? And he said, I don't want to talk about it.

And I was like, boom.

Write that down. Someone write that down.

[Unclear audio at 00:11:26–00:11:28]

That's it. And the location for the record, um, the recording sounds really interesting as well. You've described it as looking like a nineties movie set of a washed up office building in South Yarra and sort of knowing that the building itself is like set for demolition. It's not there anymore. It's not there anymore. It's not there. You can't even go there. Yeah. It's like it never existed. Did knowing that the space sort of would soon be gone influence your mindset at all during those recording sessions?

I think so. Cause it's weird to go into a space when you know, it's going to not be there anymore. It's kind of like when you think about time and how short it is not to get on that level, but, um, yeah, it was cool. Like the days were numbered there. So we had to just be, be in it. Yeah. Get the record done. Get the record done. Yeah. And the, the sort of the aura was kind of threatening in there.

If, if all the lights were all on, all the lights were on fluorescent white lights. It was, there were like still computers, like old computers. It was very weird, but cool, cool energy. Yeah. Threatening, but cool. It's gone now, but it's gone. Yeah. So do you think that sense of pilgrimage? Do you think that like sense of transience makes its way like, yeah, onto the record? Yeah, I think so. Yeah. That's a good word. I like that one.

[Unclear audio at 00:12:46–00:12:50]

Well, I want to say a very big thank you to our guests today, Morgan and Kate from Acopia for dropping by and, uh, having a chat with me ahead of the sold out shows at, uh, the Night Cat next Friday. Uh, the record is Blush Response. We're going to lift a track from it. The one we were just talking about called Talk About It. Thanks so much, guys. Thank you for having us. No worries.
